accroche: Waiting to get two candies would predict success. The 2018 replication measures something else.
contenu_vulgarise:
A four-year-old child, a marshmallow placed in front of him, and an instruction: if you wait until I come back without eating it, you will get two. The experimenter leaves. Some hold out for fifteen minutes, others for fifteen seconds.

Walter Mischel ran these experiments at Stanford starting in the late 1960s. The result that made them famous came later: in 1990, a follow-up showed that the children who had waited the longest did better in adolescence. The conclusion seems self-evident: the ability to delay a reward would be an early and decisive trait.

It became a commonplace of self-help and parenting advice.

## The Replication

In 2018, Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan, and Haonan Quan published in *Psychological Science* a conceptual replication on a sample far larger and far more diverse than Mischel's, whose children came mostly from the Stanford campus, that is, from families of academics.

The association is still there. But it is about half as strong as in the original studies. And above all, it shrinks by two thirds once family background, the mother's level of education, and early cognitive abilities are taken into account.

In other words: much of what the marshmallow measured was not the child's willpower. It was his situation.

## Why It Makes Sense

Waiting is rational when you have reasons to trust. A child whose environment is predictable, where promises are kept and food is never uncertain, has every reason to be patient: the second candy will come.

A child for whom none of this is a given has every reason to take what is there, right away. His behavior is not a character flaw. It is an accurate reading of his environment.

The test therefore does not measure only an aptitude. It also measures an experience of the world.

## What This Shifts

The marshmallow story appeals because it is individual: an inner quality, detectable at age four, that would decide an entire life. The revised version is less marketable, and distinctly more useful: most of what was taken for a character trait points back to material conditions.

This shift changes what can be done with it. One does not train a child in patience the way one builds up an arm. One can, however, make his environment more reliable.

repere.texte: In the 2018 replication, the association between waiting and success is half as strong as in the original studies, and shrinks by two thirds once family background is taken into account.

carte.punch: The marshmallow test measured background more than willpower.
carte.idee: The 2018 replication, on a far larger sample, finds an effect half as strong, shrunk by two thirds once family background is taken into account. Waiting is rational when you have reasons to trust.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The replication, with the details of the control variables.

quiz.question: What did the 2018 replication of the marshmallow test show?
choix: That the patient children actually did worse in adolescence
That the link disappears entirely once the experimental protocol is changed
That waiting time could not be measured reliably at age four
That the link remains but collapses once family background is taken into account
quiz.explication: The association did not disappear: it is about half as strong as reported, and shrinks by two thirds when family background and early cognitive abilities are controlled for. The difference is decisive: waiting largely reflects the reliability of the child's environment, not a single personal quality.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where did the children in Mischel's original experiments of the late 1960s mainly come from?
choix: From very low-income families, recruited in disadvantaged neighborhoods of Stanford
Mostly from families of academics on the Stanford campus
From a representative sample of the American population as a whole
From California orphanages partnered with the university
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Mischel's original sample came mostly from the Stanford campus, that is, from families of academics, far less diverse than the larger sample of the 2018 replication.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the text, why does a child in an unreliable environment have reason not to wait for the second marshmallow?
choix: Because he has not yet developed the cognitive abilities needed to be patient
Because impatient children statistically do better in adolescence
Because the experimental protocol does not provide a second marshmallow for some children
Because nothing guarantees him that the promise of an extra reward will be kept
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A child whose environment is unpredictable, where promises are not always kept, has reason to take what is there right away: his behavior reflects an accurate reading of his environment.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which publication reports the 1990 longitudinal follow-up that made the marshmallow test famous?
choix: Watts, Duncan, and Quan, in Psychological Science
Mischel, Ebbesen, and Zeiss, in Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Shoda, Mischel, and Peake, in Developmental Psychology
An unpublished internal report from Stanford University
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1990 follow-up that establishes the link between waiting at age four and success in adolescence was published by Shoda, Mischel, and Peake in Developmental Psychology, distinct from the original protocol and from the 2018 replication.
